title: The Expressibility of Polynomial based Attention Scheme

problem.claim: The quadratic complexity of transformer attention makes very large models impractical to train on lengthy texts or use efficiently during inference.

gap.claim: The theoretical understanding of polynomial attention, which replaces softmax with a polynomial function and uses polynomial sketching, is not yet well understood.

contributions.claim: Provides a theoretical analysis of the expressive capabilities of polynomial attention.
Characterizes a disparity between high-degree and low-degree polynomial attention using two designed datasets that differ by a significantly larger feature value.
Shows that sufficiently high-degree polynomial attention can distinguish the two datasets, whereas low-degree polynomial attention cannot effectively separate them.

author_reported_evidence.claim: With a sufficiently high degree β, a single-layer polynomial attention network can distinguish between D0 and D1.
With a low degree β, the network cannot effectively separate D0 and D1.
The analysis indicates that high-degree polynomials are more effective at amplifying large values and distinguishing between datasets.

narrative_sequence.summary: LLMs have improved daily life across domains including healthcare and education.
Quadratic attention complexity limits efficient training and inference for very large models and lengthy texts.
Polynomial attention offers a speed-oriented alternative, but its theoretical behavior remains insufficiently understood.
The paper analyzes polynomial-attention expressiveness and contrasts high- and low-degree behavior using two constructed datasets.
High-degree polynomial attention separates the datasets while low-degree attention does not effectively do so, motivating higher-degree polynomials for capturing intricate linguistic correlations.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the exact definitions of D0 and D1 beyond their differing feature magnitude.
The abstract does not provide the degree thresholds, quantitative results, baselines, or experimental evaluation details.
The abstract does not establish computational costs, generalization behavior, or performance on real language tasks.
